title: On these questions: common Rome and Reformed often agree in substance; caveats
source_text: LIX. Caeterum quod diximus, in multis illis ante expositis quaestionibus, Scholam Romanam in re ipsa cum Reformata consentire, etsi verbis multum inter se contendant, verum, quod has praecise quaestiones attinet, reperietur, si quis communem & solennem Scholae Romanae doctrinam, cum ea quae communi calculo in Scholis quoque nostris recepta est, comparet. Non negamus autem, quin privati Doctores nonnulli, circa praedictas quaestiones, in utraque Schola, quaedam singularia doceant, quae ab adversae partis sententia non verbis tantum, sed reipsa discrepant. Nec enim affirmare volumus ipsam communem doctrinam Ecclesiae Romanae, in aliis controversiis, non pugnare cum illa eadem veritate, quam hic agnoscere coguntur, & eam, ex consequenti saltem, non evertere. Denique fatendum est etiam iis, qui recte in hac parte sentiunt, inter disputandum multa excidere, in quibus sibi ipsis contradicere videntur, & quae benigno egent interprete, ut ad bonum & commodum sensum revocari queant.
pass_a_gloss: For the rest, what we have said—that in many of those questions set forth above the Roman School agrees with the Reformed in the thing itself, even if they contend much among themselves in words—will truly be found, as concerns these precise questions, if anyone compares the common and solemn doctrine of the Roman School with that which by common ballot is also received in our Schools. We do not deny, however, that some private Doctors, around the aforesaid questions, in either School teach certain singular things which differ from the adverse party's opinion not in words only but in the thing itself. Nor indeed do we wish to affirm that the common doctrine of the Roman Church itself, in other controversies, does not fight with that same truth which they are compelled to acknowledge here, and does not overturn it, at least by consequence. Finally it must be confessed even of those who think rightly in this part that in disputing many things slip out in which they seem to contradict themselves, and which need a benign interpreter so that they can be recalled to a good and fitting sense.
pass_b_english: On these precise heads, common Rome and Reformed often agree in substance despite word-fights.
Caveats: private oddities; other Roman loci may still undercut this truth; even sound disputants need a benign reading.

lemmas.gloss: to agree in the thing itself

choices.why: Closes Quomodo Roman coda with irenic method + limits.
rejected: full dogmatic identity of the two schools
